Abstract
As the demand for computing power continues to rise, it is diﬃcult for a single type
of computing device or architecture to satisfy the current situation. Diversity and
heterogeneity are becoming more and more popular. Seamlessly integrating the
realms of high performance computing and quantum computing, and harnessing
their collective potential, has emerged as a consensus approach to eﬀectively address
the pressing need for increased computing power. In the emerging computing
scenario, various diﬀerent types of computing devices have super-heterogeneous
characteristics, and there are signiﬁcant diﬀerences in computational principles,
programming models, parallelism, etc. Eﬀectively harnessing these disparate
resources and achieving a uniﬁed programming paradigm have become urgent
imperatives. To address the above problems, this paper introduces QCCP, a taskﬂow
programming model that enables eﬃcient collaborative computing between
classical computers and quantum computers. QCCP establishes a uniﬁed
programming abstraction, shields the super-heterogeneous characteristics of the
underlying network and hardware, and supports ﬂexible scheduling for diﬀerent
computational backends. The experimental results indicate that QCCP can support
the processing of hybrid classical-quantum applications with diverse program
structures. In particular, QCCP reveals its immense potential and superiority in tackling
real-world challenges, speciﬁcally in the realm of quantum circuit cutting and
reconstruction.
Keywords: Super-heterogeneous; Programming abstraction; Programming
paradigm; Classical-quantum collaborative computation

The rapid development of information technology constantly puts forward higher re-

puting in collaborative work. Based on the above analysis, it can be expected that for the
promising large-scale complex computational problems, classical-quantum collaborative
computing [14] will be a highly potential solution. It is possible to try to integrate classical
computing hardware with quantum computing hardware to construct a new computing
system with the ability to deal with multiple types of complex tasks.
Classical-quantum collaborative computing is a novel computing paradigm that ex-
hibits notable distinctions from single classical computing, single quantum computing,
and traditional heterogeneous computing [15]. Within this emerging computing scenario,
there exist classical-classical heterogeneity, quantum-quantum heterogeneity, as well as
classical-quantum heterogeneity, as shown in Fig. 1. The super-heterogeneous character-
istics among various computing devices are reﬂected not only in the fundamental diver-
gence of computing principles but also in the diﬀerence of programming models and par-
allel approaches. Additionally, the current manufacturing process for quantum comput-

To solve the above problems, this paper proposes a new taskﬂow programming model
QCCP for emerging computing scenario. QCCP allows users to customize the granular-
ity of computing tasks using pre-set programming interface, reducing the programming
diﬃculty. It can also convert hybrid computing tasks into directed acyclic graph (DAG),
support uniﬁed task scheduling for multiple computing backends, and promote the full
utilization of various computing resources. Moreover, QCCP provides important support
for the growing classic-quantum collaborative computing system.
More speciﬁcally, the main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:
• We delved into the development trend of hybrid classical-quantum computing and
proposed a novel distributed computing scenario prospectively, which is composed of
multiple classical and quantum computing devices. All computing devices are
considered equal and there is no strict division between master and slave.
• Aiming at the issues of uniﬁed programming and scheduling of hybrid computing
resources in this scenario, we design and implement a taskﬂow programming model
named QCCP. By establishing a uniﬁed programming abstraction, QCCP can
transform hybrid computing tasks into DAGs and supports ﬂexible scheduling across
diﬀerent computing backends, eﬀectively shielding the super-heterogeneous
characteristics of the underlying network and hardware.
• Based on the mini-benchmark, we ﬁrstly verify that QCCP can support hybrid
classical-quantum applications with diﬀerent program structures. Furthermore, we
explore the application of QCCP in real-world problems such as quantum circuit
cutting and reconstruction. Taking the quantum circuit of quantum approximate

2 Background knowledge
2.1 The emerging computing scenario
Heterogeneous computing is a development trend and has shown signiﬁcant advantages
in solving practical problems. In the ﬁeld of classical heterogeneous computing, the col-
laboration between the central processing unit (CPU) and the graphics processing unit
(GPU) is a very typical case. For example, in graphics rendering or deep learning training
problems, the CPU often calls speciﬁc application programming interfaces (APIs) to send
relevant commands and data to the GPU. The GPU has more processing units than CPU
and is very suitable for parallelizing large-scale computing. These years, the application-
speciﬁc integrated circuit (ASIC) is becoming increasingly popular, which is commonly
used to perform computing tasks together with CPU. Typical practical application is the
fast synchronous video technology of Intel. For the coordination problem of CPU and
quantum processing unit (QPU), theoretically speaking, the emergence of this new com-
puting mode can be considered as another breakthrough in the computing power revolu-
tion. In other words, this indicates that the transition from heterogeneous computing stage
to super-heterogeneous computing has begun. Although quantum computer and classical
computer have great diﬀerences in calculation principle and actual operation process, the
successful experience in classical heterogeneous computing can provide useful reference
for classic-quantum collaborative computing.
Up to now, quantum computing resources are still relatively scarce and expensive. Most
researchers need to rely on quantum computing cloud platforms [17]. In this way, the
communication workload between quantum and classical computing devices is a major
obstacle aﬀecting the overall computing performance. With the maturity of quantum com-
puters, a new computing route that integrates quantum and classical computing devices is
getting more and more attention. In fact, there have been some related works around this
idea, which can be mainly divided into two categories: quantum-centric supercomputing
and classic-centric quantum-accelerated supercomputing. IBM is a typical representative
of the former, which combines QPU, CPU, GPU and other computing resources through
quantum and classical communication networks in the hardware layer to form a new com-
puting architecture. In the software layer, quantum and classical computing resources are
managed through a software stack mainly composed of Quantum Serverless. The latter,
represented by NVIDIA and the European Quantum Community, regards quantum com-
puters as accelerators in heterogeneous systems at the hardware level and incorporates

In this computing scenario, we introduce the concept of peer computing, which means that
quantum computing resources and classical computing resources are regarded as equal.
The hybrid classical-quantum applications will be disassembled into multiple subtasks
and executed on diﬀerent types of computing devices. Considering the current quantum
computing is still in the NISQ era, this paper is dedicated to designing a series of software
means to shield the diﬀerences between multiple types of computing devices, support the
ﬂexible combination and utilization of multiple computing resources and ensure the eﬀec-
tive communication between quantum and classical systems, striving to achieve eﬃcient
classical-quantum collaborative computing.
2.2 Working mechanism of superconducting quantum computer
Limited by the current theoretical and technological level, the quantum computer in the
NISQ era is not a device that can independently complete the computational task, but
a heterogeneous computing system with exponential acceleration for speciﬁc problems.
As shown in Fig. 3, the whole computing system mainly consists of the host computer,
measurement and control equipment (MCE) and QPU. The host computer is essentially a
classical computer equipped with quantum compiler, measurement and control software
(MCS). When submitting a quantum task to the host computer, the quantum circuit will

be transformed into optimized quantum assembly language (e.g. OpenQASM) through
the compiler module in the host computer. Then the QASM ﬁle will be processed by the
MCS and converted into digital signals with waveform control information. Next, the dig-
ital signals are sent to the MCE and converted into the measurement and control wave-
forms, which will ultimately be used to control the qubits to achieve the transformation of
quantum states. When the measurement operation is performed, the MCE is responsible
for the conversion of analog signals to digital signals, and then the MCS processes the ﬁnal
measurement results.
The working mechanism of quantum computer actually reﬂects the fusion characteris-
tics of classical computing and quantum computing. However, there are some obvious dif-
ferences with the traditional classical computer: Firstly, the classical computing capability
of quantum computer is usually limited. Secondly, the classical computing part of whole
process is usually some simple data processing work, i.e. classical pre-processing and clas-
sical post-processing, while the core computing part occurs at the QPU. Thirdly, the quan-
tum computing has the characteristic of process in memory. The qubit is also responsible
for data storage while performing computational tasks, which means that when running
quantum tasks on a quantum computer, it will deﬁnitely go through the three steps, i.e.
classical pre-processing, quantum processing, and classical post-processing. Furthermore,
the order of these three steps cannot be exchanged. For users, they only need to focus on
the quantum circuit construction and submission. The working details of the MCS, MCE,
and the QPU are invisible and uncontrollable. Theoretically, the precise controllability
of the host computer within a quantum computing system implies the potential for eﬃ-

3 Programming model
Integrating multiple quantum and classical computing devices has become one of the con-
sensus technological approaches to adapt to the growing demand for computing power in
the future. However, due to the vastly diﬀerent physical principles between the two types of
computing modes, there are signiﬁcant diﬀerences in terms of computation, communica-
tion, control, storage, and other aspects. In order to achieve the goal of collaborative com-
puting in the emerging computing scenario, this paper proposes a taskﬂow programming
model that can disassemble and encapsulate hybrid applications in terms of tasks, which is
conducive to the rapid coding and development of hybrid classical-quantum applications.
In the following, this section highlights some technical details about the QCCP. Firstly, the
label model for computing backends is deﬁned in Sect. 3.1. In Sect. 3.2, the DAG abstrac-
tion for hybrid applications is introduced. In Sect. 3.3, the principles of task partitioning
and orchestration are elaborated. Finally, we give an example for hybrid classical-quantum
coding and analyze its execution process.
3.1 Label model
The emerging computing scenario is essentially a distributed computing environment
consisting of multiple types of classical and quantum computing backends. To achieve
scientiﬁc management and scheduling, an eﬀective solution is to construct a label model
with the computational attributes of backends. Assuming there are m classical computing
backends and n quantum computing backends in the current computing environment,
which can be represented as C = (c1,c2,...,cm), Q = (q1,q2,...,qn), and then the labels set
can be represented as L = (lc1,lc2,...,lcm,lq1,lq1,...lqn), where lci represents the label of
classical backend ci, and lqj represents the label of quantum backend qj. The basic in-
formation, such as the IP address, number of qubits, etc., of the computing backend is
revealed in the above labels.
3.2 DAG abstraction
It is a common programming paradigm to write functions one by one and then use them
in combination within the main() to achieve diﬀerent goals. This approach not only facil-
itates creating a well-organized program structure but also enhances the readability and
maintainability of the code. Therefore, we persist in embracing this proven programming
paradigm within the design of QCCP. Considering the potential and beneﬁts oﬀered by
the graph computation model [18] in classical computing, we integrate the DAG model
into QCCP to implement programming abstractions eﬀectively. As shown in Fig. 4, the hy-
brid classical-quantum application can be converted into a graph denoted as G = (V,E,R),
where v ∈V denotes the task, the directed edge e ∈E denotes the dependencies between
tasks, and the mapping function R represents the mapping relationship between vertexes
in the DAG and the computing backends.
Vertex: A vertex v can represent a classical computing task (will be executed by classical
computing devices) or a quantum computing task (will be executed by quantum comput-
ing devices). In the code, a vertex is equal to a function decorated with @qccp.ctask or

3.3 Task partitioning and orchestration
QCCP provides a ﬂexible programming method that enables the organization of complex
data stream processing into taskﬂow and supports various hybrid classical-quantum pro-
gram structures. Speciﬁcally, QCCP oﬀers a set of compilation directives (referred to as
decorators in Python) that users can explicitly specify when coding, which serve as the
main reference for task partitioning.
@qccp.ctask: A classical computing task usually exists as a function. Adding this deco-
rator to a function means completing the speciﬁc deﬁnition of its functionality.
@qccp.qtask: The function decorated by this decorator is essentially a quantum com-
puting task, which mainly includes the construction and submission process of quantum
circuit when coding.
@qccp.taskﬂow: Typically used as a decorator of the main function. The decorated func-
tion describes the composition structure of the taskﬂow. Additionally, it invokes the func-
tions decorated by @qccp.ctask and @qccp.qtask, representing a taskﬂow that can be trans-
formed into a sequence of classical tasks and quantum tasks.

4 Implementation
This section describes some implementation details in QCCP. Currently, many popular
quantum programming languages (e.g. Qiskit, QPanda) use python as the host language.
Besides, the quantum circuits built based on above languages can be easily converted into
OpenQASM sequences that are easily recognized by the quantum hardware. Considering
compatibility and applicability, we also develop the QCCP based on python.
4.1 Execution overview
In the following, a taskﬂow execution model based on QCCP is presented, as shown in
Fig. 8. From the perspective of distributed collaboration, there are the following key steps
in the execution of hybrid computing tasks, including task dispatching, local execution,
intermediate result collection, and result post-processing.
Task dispatching: The hybrid task will be converted into a DAG with execution logic
information after partitioning and orchestration. Based on this step, each task within the
taskﬂow needs to be assigned to the target computing backend for execution. Speciﬁcally,
the functions and necessary input parameters are serialized into a .pkl ﬁle with the cloud-
pickle library. Then the taskﬂow scheduler dispatches the task to the target computing
backend.
Local execution: When a computing node receives a picked task, its own Local scheduler
will automatically create a worker process to take over the task, which means that the
worker process will use the computational resources of the node to execute the assigned
task. Speciﬁcally, it will ﬁrst perform a deserialization operation to restore the task and
input parameters, and then perform the corresponding computational operations locally.
It should be pointed out that when executing quantum tasks, the host computer in the
quantum computing system needs to call interface such as quantum_task_submit() to
implement the submission and executing of quantum circuits. The dataﬂow during this
process has been revealed in Fig. 3.

4.2 Two-level hierarchical scheduling
As mentioned in Sect. 2.1, the programming model designed in this paper needs to be
able to shield the diﬀerences between diﬀerent computing devices in emerging scenarios,
and ensure the ﬂexible invocation of multiple types of computing resources for orderly
execution of task DAG. However, existing classical and quantum computing devices have
signiﬁcant diﬀerences in terms of working principles and software ecosystems, which pose
signiﬁcant challenges for hybrid task scheduling.
To meet above requirements, we design a two-level hierarchical scheduling mechanism,
including global scheduler (i.e., taskﬂow scheduler) and per-node local scheduler (i.e., local
scheduler). The taskﬂow scheduler focuses on the orchestration and dispatch of taskﬂow.
Once the DAG is established, the task will be sent to the corresponding execution ma-
chine. After the computation is completed, it ensures the ordered data transmission be-
tween adjacent computing tasks, thereby guaranteeing that the entire taskﬂow can be run
in the topological order. The local scheduler is implemented based on the Dask framework
[19], aiming to maximize the utilization of computing resources. The local scheduler has
two working modes depending on the target execution machine. For classical computing
devices, when receiving tasks from the taskﬂow scheduler, the local scheduler automati-
cally creates the worker processes, which are responsible for executing the Ctask module.
For task scheduling on quantum computing devices, the situation is slightly diﬀerent. The
host computer of quantum computing system also automatically creates the worker pro-
cesses. During the submission and execution of the quantum circuit, the worker process
directly communicates with the MCE by calling the interface of MCS, thereby indirectly
achieving control and data reading from the QPU. Based on the above mechanism, we have
achieved organic unity in global and local task scheduling, while minimizing the impact
on the original working modes of various types of computing devices.
4.3 Asynchronous and parallel
To improve the execution eﬃciency of taskﬂow, QCCP introduces the Coroutine mecha-
nism [20]. These task modules decorated with @qccp.ctask and @qccp.qtask are executed
on the corresponding target machine with async/await scheme, which means the user-
agnostic asynchronous execution can be achieved without manually rewriting the code.
In the DAG, each vertex (i.e. task) corresponds to a function. When the data dependency
of any task is satisﬁed, it can be executed asynchronously. Among them, the output of a
task may be the input of multiple tasks. Similarly, when the common data dependency of
multiple tasks is satisﬁed, they can be executed in parallel (e.g. v4 and v5 in Fig. 8), even if
they are on diﬀerent computing devices (e.g. v2 and v3 and in Fig. 8).

4.4 Node communication
In the classical-quantum collaborative computing scenario, node communication refers to
the process of data transmission and communication between diﬀerent worker processes
on diﬀerent computing nodes, as well as on the same computing node. These two situa-
tions are called intra-node communication and inter-node communication respectively.
Intra-node Communication. When the taskﬂow scheduler sends a task to the target ex-
ecution device, the local scheduler typically creates a corresponding number of worker
processes based on the number of logical cores. If the task contains more than one func-
tion modules and there are data dependencies between the functions, then the data com-
munication between these worker processes is required when executing. Recognizing this
crucial requirement, QCCP leverages the TCP Sockets to implement this communication
paradigm.
Inter-node Communication. If the taskﬂow scheduler sends tasks to diﬀerent computing
devices and there are data dependencies between these tasks, then the data communica-
tion between worker processes on diﬀerent computing devices is required. Considering
the software environment diﬀerences between classical and quantum computing devices,
as well as the diverse requirements for complex data processing in collaborative comput-
ing process, QCCP adopts a method of temporarily storing pickled ﬁles in the ﬁle system,
which has advantages such as cross-platform compatibility, ﬂexibility, and long-term stor-
age.

In order to analyze the execution eﬃciency of the hybrid classical-quantum program after

5.2 Real-world applications: quantum circuit cutting and reconstruction
5.2.1 Problem description
In the era of NISQ, the quantum computing resource is very limited, which makes it dif-
ﬁcult for many existing quantum algorithms to achieve ideal results on real machines. In
response to this problem, scholars have proposed an eﬀective solution, namely, quantum
circuit cutting and reconstruction. With this method, the large-scale quantum circuit is
divided into several sub-circuits according to certain rules, then these sub-circuits will be
executed in various quantum computers with limited qubits to get a set of results. Next,
the reconstruction technology is used to perform classical post-processing on the previ-
ously obtained results, and ﬁnally obtain approximate theoretical results of the original
large-scale circuit.
Quantum circuit cutting and reconstruction is a typical hybrid classical-quantum com-
puting application. which can be divided into three stages based on its operational charac-
teristics, circuit analysis and cutting, sub-circuit compilation and execution, and classical
post-processing. Among them, the ﬁrst and third steps belong to classical computing mod-
ules, and the second step belongs to quantum computing module. The whole computing
task is naturally suitable for execution in the emerging computing scenario mentioned in
this paper.

5.2.3 Taskﬂow execution scheme
Based on the computing environment, the next step is to provide a taskﬂow execution
scheme for circuit cutting and reconstruction, as shown in Fig. 15.
The detailed computing process is as follows:
(1) Submit relevant information of the original quantum circuit to node M1. Then, this
node analyzes it and performs circuit cutting operations based on the ILOG CPLEX
Interactive Optimizer and CutQC tools. Next, the sub-circuits information and
initial quantum state information are sent to the quantum computing nodes M2 and
M3.
(2) The two quantum computing nodes run the sub-circuits respectively, and then send
the running results to the classical computing node M1.
(3) The classical post-processing is performed by M1, which is responsible for
reconstructing the execution results of sub-circuits to obtain the approximate
theoretical results of the original large-scale circuit.

Based on the current development status of quantum computing, it is evident that large-
scale quantum computing is still on the horizon. As we strive to reach this goal, quantum
circuit cutting and reconstruction emerges as a pivotal technology to enable us to real-
ize quantum computing in an indirect manner. Speciﬁcally, it serves as a bridge between
quantum computing resources and classical computing infrastructure. As the complexity
and scale of quantum circuits continue to expand, it becomes increasingly vital to comple-
ment them with robust classical computing capabilities. The demands placed on classical
computing systems are expected to escalate alongside the growth of quantum circuits. In
this regard, the collaborative eﬀorts of supercomputers are likely to be essential in sup-
porting quantum circuit cutting and reconstruction. By design, QCCP aims to facilitate
scientiﬁc management and the eﬀective allocation of diverse computing resources. It em-
powers us to orchestrate the complex interplay between quantum and classical computing
in a systematic and optimized manner. With this in mind, we ﬁrmly believe that QCCP
holds immense potential for wide-ranging applications in the realm of high-performance
computing.

6 Related work
As one of the most disruptive new computing technologies, quantum computing has
demonstrated its powerful computational capabilities at the theoretical level and has con-
tinuously achieved innovative breakthroughs in engineering. However, current quantum
computing is unable to independently complete complex computing tasks, which presents
a signiﬁcant opportunity for the integration of high-performance computing and quantum
computing.
In terms of hardware, there have been some advances in the integration and construc-
tion of classical-quantum computing facilities in recent years. For example, in Novem-
ber 2021, Dell collaborated with IonQ to achieve a small-scale hybrid classical-quantum
computing platform by combining Dell PowerEdge R740xd servers with IonQ’s simula-
tion engine and QPU. To meet the computing demands of more complex tasks, the J˘ulich
Supercomputing Centre (JSC) [24] plans to connect its High-Performance Computing
(HPC) system based on a modular supercomputing architecture (MSA) environment with
diﬀerent quantum computers through the Uniﬁed Quantum Computing Infrastructure
(JUNIQ). In November 2022, the Technical Research Centre of Finland (VTT), CSC-IT
Center for Science, and Aalto University connected the quantum computer HELMI with
the LUMI supercomputer within the Finnish Quantum Computing Infrastructure (FiQCI)
framework. However, as the hardware infrastructure continues to develop and improve,
some key technical issues have emerged, such as monitoring and managing multiple types
of computing devices and ﬂexibly utilizing diﬀerent computing resources.
Furthermore, the software ecosystem for classical-quantum collaborative computing
scenarios is of signiﬁcant importance [25]. Traditional heterogeneous programming mod-
els such as OpenACC, OpenMP, CUDA, and SYCL are relatively mature, but they are
mainly good at loop-based parallelism based on CPUs/GPUs architectures [26] and can-
not directly handle hybrid classical-quantum taskﬂows. With the development of quan-
tum computing, new hybrid classical-quantum programming models/frameworks have
emerged, such as XACC [27], CUDA Quantum [28], and Qiskit [29]. Among them, XACC
and QODA support classic-centric hybrid classical-quantum computing, while Qiskit
supports quantum-centric hybrid classical-quantum computing. These technologies dif-
fer from the peer computing concept introduced in the proposed QCCP. Additionally, they
also have a common limitation, which is that we can only obtain the real machine resources
from quantum cloud service. On the one hand, this approach has limited interfaces for
user programming, and on the other hand, it has signiﬁcant instability. After submitting
quantum tasks, users may face unpredictable queuing and latency problems, which seri-
ously aﬀect the eﬃciency of hybrid computing tasks. The application computing scenario
of QCCP is mainly a distributed environment formed by the interconnection of multiple
classical and quantum computing devices. We have fully considered the working mecha-
nism of superconducting quantum computer in the NISQ era, as well as the characteristics
of collaborative computing with multiple types of computing backends during the design
process, ensuring the eﬃcient execution of various hybrid applications in the emerging
computing scenario. We envision that with the gradual maturity of quantum computing
technology, this computing mode will be an inevitable trend for the fusion of classical and
quantum computing in the future.

7 Conclusion and outlook
Classical-quantum collaborative computing is a widely recognized ﬁeld. From recent re-
search trends [30, 31], the integration of QPUs and HPC has overcome the challenges of
cloud connectivity and demonstrated veriﬁcation in speciﬁc problems. With the growing
maturity of modular integration technology, future classical-quantum collaborative com-
puting systems are expected to develop towards tightly coupled and large-scale directions.
In this trend, it becomes increasingly important to eﬃciently utilize various classical and
quantum computing resources to solve problems that are diﬃcult or impossible to solve
with a single type of resource.
To address the challenges of classical-quantum collaborative computing, the QCCP has
explored and innovated at the software stack level. Its main focus is on scientiﬁc con-
trol and eﬃcient collaboration of multiple types of computing devices. QCCP builds a
bridge between hybrid applications and complex underlying operations, while minimizing
changes to the existing working methods and software ecosystems of various computing
devices. More importantly, it establishes a uniﬁed programming abstraction that shields
the heterogeneity of underlying networks and hardware, facilitating the convenient ex-
ecution of upper-layer hybrid applications and the eﬃcient management and utilization
of multiple types of computing resources. Based on this programming model, users only
need to follow the corresponding programming rules to write classical-quantum hybrid
programs without worrying about the underlying resource scheduling, data communica-
tion, and other implementation details. This provides users with a more convenient devel-
opment and usage experience while improving the utilization eﬃciency of multiple types
of computing resources. However, the computing scenario emphasized in this paper is
essentially a distributed classical-quantum collaborative computation based on classical
communication networks. And QCCP is only one possible implementation solution for
programming model issues in this computing scenario. Our research ﬁndings can provide
insights for the design of classical-quantum collaborative computing system. As there is
currently no standard answer to the integration of classical and quantum computing, it is
still necessary to continue exploring how to program portably and eﬃciently utilize vari-
ous types of classical and quantum computing resources.
In the foreseeable future, the blueprint for emerging computing scenario will expand
and become clearer. Quantum computers with diﬀerent technological routes will continue
to focus on achieving specialized quantum machines in the next ﬁve years or longer, with
the emphasis on continuously optimization and improving issues such as qubit scale, qubit
quality, and error correction. Simultaneously, the deep integration of quantum computing
with the classical supercomputing system heralds an important direction for the develop-
ment of the advanced computing ﬁeld, which will reshape our computing capabilities and
technological architecture. Prospectively, more and more computing centers will deploy
both classical supercomputers and quantum computers. Distributed quantum comput-
ing [32], along with quantum communication network [33] technologies, can construct
a more secure and eﬃcient communication channel between geographically dispersed
computational centers. This oﬀers novel solutions for tackling complex problems in the
real world. At that time, the classical Internet and the quantum Internet will coexist and
operate concurrently [34]. Under this heterogeneous network structure, the collaborative
operation of multiple types of computing devices becomes signiﬁcantly more intricate.

According to the above, there are several directions for improvement in the ongoing re-
search work. On one hand, we will continue to focus on the distributed classical-quantum
collaborative computing based on classical communication networks. This involves ana-
lyzing the structure and computational characteristics of hybrid classical-quantum appli-
cations, optimizing the collaborative computing process, and enhancing computational
eﬃciency and accuracy. On the other hand, taking into account the coexistence of the
classical Internet and the quantum Internet, we aim to support a wider variety of resource
allocation and task assignment strategies, and strive to achieve more ﬂexible and eﬃcient
classical-quantum collaborative computing.

Abstract: As the demand for computing power continues to rise, it is diﬃcult for a single type of computing device or architecture to satisfy the current situation. Diversity and heterogeneity are becoming more and more popular. Seamlessly integrating the realms of high performance computing and quantum computing, and harnessing their collective potential, has emerged as a consensus approach to eﬀectively address the pressing need for increased computing power. In the emerging computing scenario, various diﬀerent types of computing devices have super-heterogeneous characteristics, and there are signiﬁcant diﬀerences in computational principles, programming models, parallelism, etc. Eﬀectively harnessing these disparate resources and achieving a uniﬁed programming paradigm have become urgent imperatives. To address the above problems, this paper introduces QCCP, a taskﬂow programming model that enables eﬃcient collaborative computing between classical computers and quantum computers. QCCP establishes a uniﬁed programming abstraction, shields the super-heterogeneous characteristics of the underlying network and hardware, and supports ﬂexible scheduling for diﬀerent computational backends. The experimental results indicate that QCCP can support the processing of hybrid classical-quantum applications with diverse program structures. In particular, QCCP reveals its immense potential and superiority in tackling real-world challenges, speciﬁcally in the realm of quantum circuit cutting and reconstruction.
